lpc.story.celerinus-writes-to-lucian.telling_short:
Celerinus was one of our confessors, a man who had been imprisoned and had not denied Christ. He wrote to Lucian, another confessor still in prison.

"Grieve with me over my sister's death, a death of the spirit," he wrote. "In this time of ruin she has fallen away from Christ." He also asked the martyrs' pardon for two women Lucian knew, Numeria and Candida.

Lucian granted the request in the name of the martyrs, with one condition. Each case was to be set before the bishop and the sin openly confessed. Then, he asked, let the women have peace.
lpc.story.celerinus-writes-to-lucian.telling_medium:
Celerinus was one of our confessors, a man who had been imprisoned and had not denied Christ. He wrote to Lucian, another confessor, who was still in prison.

"Grieve with me over my sister's death, a death of the spirit," he wrote. "In this time of ruin she has fallen away from Christ." He would weep, he said, until help came through Lucian or the martyrs.

He also asked the martyrs' pardon for Numeria and Candida. He pointed to their repentance and their good works. Candida had given gifts so that she would not have to sacrifice. "So I know she has not sacrificed." Still, both letters call what the women did a great sin.

Lucian answered from the prison, where the confessors were to die by hunger and thirst. "But now we have reached the brightness itself," he wrote.

He granted the request in the name of the martyr Paulus and the other martyrs, with one condition. Each case was to be set before the bishop and the sin openly confessed. Then, he asked, let the women have peace.

lpc.story.hundred-thousand-sesterces.telling_short:
Word came that our brothers and sisters had been carried off and were held captive among barbarians. Eight bishops in Numidia wrote to Cyprian about it.

His argument was not about charity but about who the captives were. He quoted Paul: "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Then he drew the conclusion. "So Christ is to be seen in our captive brothers."

Our clergy and people gave the money. "So we have sent you a sum of one hundred thousand sesterces."
lpc.story.hundred-thousand-sesterces.telling_medium:
Word came that our brothers and sisters had been carried off and were held captive among barbarians. Eight bishops in Numidia wrote to Cyprian about it: Januarius, Maximus, Proculus, Victor, Modianus, Nemesianus, Nampulus and Honoratus.

His reply opens without composure. "With great grief of mind, and not without tears, dearest brothers, I have read your letter."

His argument was not about charity but about who the captives were. He quoted Paul: "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Then he drew the conclusion. "So Christ is to be seen in our captive brothers."

He named the test this set for us. "Will each of us do for another what he would want done for himself, if he were held captive among barbarians?"

"So we have sent you a sum of one hundred thousand sesterces." It came from the gifts of our clergy and people. He thanked the bishops for offering us "fruitful fields in which to sow the seeds of our hope."

lpc.story.the-death-of-cyprian.heart: Our great bishop Cyprian was executed on 14 September 258, and his people kept watch and cried out to die with him. Two early texts tell his death; they agree on the core and differ on who tied the cloths over his eyes.

lpc.story.the-death-of-cyprian.telling_short:
Our great bishop Cyprian was executed on 14 September 258. His deacon Pontius told it in a saint's life. The Acta, a Christian compilation built around his hearings, tells it too.

On his last night, "the whole people kept watch before the officer's door," Pontius writes. In the Acta, sentenced as an enemy of the gods, Cyprian answered, "Thanks be to God." The brothers cried, "Let us be beheaded with him too."

The texts differ on the cloth over his eyes. Pontius says he bound them himself. In the Acta, two clergy, both named Julianus, tied them. So the blessed Cyprian suffered martyrdom.
lpc.story.the-death-of-cyprian.telling_medium:
Our great bishop Cyprian was executed on 14 September 258. His deacon Pontius told it in a saint's life. The Acta, a Christian compilation built around his hearings, tells it too.

On his last night, "the whole people kept watch before the officer's door," Pontius writes.

The sentence called Cyprian a standard-bearer of the sect and an enemy of the gods. In the Acta, Cyprian answered, "Thanks be to God." The brothers cried, "Let us be beheaded with him too." Pontius calls the people blessed for suffering with their bishop.

In the field of Sextus, the Acta says, Cyprian took off his cloak and knelt in prayer. He told his people to give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces.

The texts differ on the cloth over his eyes. Pontius says he bound them himself. In the Acta, two clergy, both named Julianus, tied them.

Pontius adds that people climbed into the trees to see, as with Zacchaeus. In his telling, the executioner's fingers trembled until the hour of glory strengthened his hand from above. So, in the Acta, the blessed Cyprian suffered martyrdom.

lpc.story.the-plague-and-the-enemies.telling_short:
Our deacon Pontius was there. He tells it in his life of our bishop, written in praise of the man who preached.

"Afterwards a dreadful plague broke out," he wrote. "Everyone shuddered and fled, and shunned the contagion. They wickedly put out their own people."

Our bishop Cyprian gathered us in one place and preached. There was nothing remarkable, he said, in caring only for our own. We must love even our enemies, and pray for those who persecute us.

Then, Pontius says, good was done to all people, not only to those of the household of faith.
lpc.story.the-plague-and-the-enemies.telling_medium:
Our deacon Pontius was there. He tells it in his life of our bishop, written in praise of the man who preached.

"Afterwards a dreadful plague broke out," he wrote. It carried off countless people every day. "Everyone shuddered and fled, and shunned the contagion. They wickedly put out their own people." All over the city lay "no longer bodies but the corpses of many."

Our bishop gathered us and preached. There was nothing remarkable, he said, in caring only for our own. We must love even our enemies, and pray for those who persecute us. God makes His sun rise and sends rain to feed the seed, and not only for His own people. "It is right for us," Cyprian said, "to live up to our birth."

Then, Pontius says, good was done to all people, not only to those of the household of faith. Many who were too poor to give money gave their own labour instead. Tobias gathered the bodies of his own race only. More was done here.

lpc.story.the-psalms-on-the-wall.telling_short:
Possidius was Augustine's friend for nearly forty years, and he was in the house at the end.

In private talk, Possidius says, Augustine often taught one thing. Even after baptism, good Christians and priests ought not leave this life without fitting repentance.

"And he did this himself in the last illness of which he died. He ordered the very few penitential Psalms of David to be copied for him. As he lay in bed during his sickness, he would look at these sheets hanging on the wall and read them. And he wept freely and constantly."
lpc.story.the-psalms-on-the-wall.telling_medium:
Possidius was Augustine's friend for nearly forty years, and he was in the house at the end. Augustine fell ill with a fever while the Vandals besieged Hippo.

Possidius says Augustine often taught one thing. Even after baptism, good Christians and priests ought not leave this life without fitting repentance.

"And he did this himself in the last illness of which he died. He ordered the very few penitential Psalms of David to be copied for him. As he lay in bed during his sickness, he would look at these sheets hanging on the wall and read them. And he wept freely and constantly."

He had preached without ceasing until that illness. While Possidius and the others stood by, watching and praying, "he slept with his fathers," in the words of Scripture. He made no will, because as a poor man of God he had nothing to make one from.

About ten days before the end, he asked that only the doctors and those bringing food come in. The request was kept, and he had that time free for prayer.
